# Data description and availability

The master uses `data/input/households.csv` and `costs.csv`, with labels and immutable checksums in `codebook.json` and `provenance.json`. All required inputs are public and included. The original source is the corrected CC BY 4.0 McIntosh–Zeitlin replication deposit, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15881329. The old restricted deposit is not used or redistributed. Source identifiers are replaced and only selected numeric household research fields are retained. The code contains no credentials, APIs, private account data, names, addresses, coordinates, dates, or recipient lists. Numeric-type checks supplement review of the selected field list; they are not a universal reidentification test.

The default route begins at an author-processed household panel. The optional reconstruction route verifies the corrected ZIP checksum, selects and transforms the panel, and extracts accounting costs. Neither route reconstructs original survey data entry and all upstream cleaning. The README makes this scope explicit. Complete 16-category food responses produce a 12-group integer score; incomplete modules retain missingness. A one-household discrepancy between the corrected panel and the original paper's baseline eligibility count is disclosed.

# Deposit and requirements

The README title begins “Data and Code for” and matches the manuscript. No affiliation is invented. The code is MIT licensed and data retain CC BY 4.0. Third-party template attribution is separate; the draft manuscript is furnished for review without an additional reuse license.

Requirements: Python 3.12.10 with pinned NumPy 2.5.2, pandas 3.0.5, SciPy 1.18.1, Matplotlib 3.11.1. Optional source extraction requires openpyxl 3.1.5. TeX is required only for PDF compilation; tested MiKTeX 25.12 and standard packages are listed. Optional Stata validation uses built-in Stata/MP 19 commands. Optional visual inspection and the clean-copy PDF-text check use PyMuPDF; their extra dependencies are disclosed. No LLM is called in any numerical step.

Tested Windows 11 x64, eight available logical processors. Default reproduction needs no GPU or network after dependencies are installed. README states practical memory/disk allowances and measured runtime. Physical RAM could not be read in the sandbox; no fabricated hardware specification is supplied. Complete master with PDF took about 19 seconds; the clean-copy run took about 16 seconds including the observation-diagnostic table.

# Code and output map

`run.py` verifies inputs and invokes estimation, exhibit construction, validation, and optional three-pass LaTeX compilation. `code/prepare_data.py` supports source reconstruction. `code/validate_stata.do` independently checks the primary mean specification. `code/render_qa.py` renders pages for manual inspection. `code/clean_check.py` runs a fresh source copy with no prior outputs.

`docs/output-map.csv` maps all eleven tables, two figures and generated empirical text macros to code locations and numerical sources. `paper/results.tex` supplies the manuscript's empirical numbers programmatically. Source design facts, theory statements and bibliography remain external or mathematical claims and are not inferred from script success.

There are no missing table or figure programs. The package exposes balance, observation, and raw distribution outputs beyond the displayed exhibits. The independent Stata check covers five diet coefficients and standard errors; no claim is made that it verifies every outcome or bootstrap result.

# Replication execution and findings

The source extraction was run on the corrected archive. Package-dependent implementation errors encountered during development (constant baseline controls, the originally global missing-baseline imputation) were fixed and logged in `docs/plan-amendments.md`. Outputs were regenerated after each substantive fix. The frozen analysis plan and amendments are retained rather than overwritten.

The complete master finished successfully. `output/validation.json` records 29 of 29 scientific/data checks passed, including policy feasibility, exact budget mixtures, all 221 primary comparisons, integer support, missing-outcome sample counts, and independent Stata agreement. Largest Python–Stata coefficient difference was below 1.3e-13 and largest standard-error difference below 5.2e-15. These are actual comparisons from the independent run, not assumed agreement.

A fresh source copy, without any existing generated outputs, reproduced all checked estimate CSVs, tables, numerical macros, policy JSON, plot PNGs and PDF page text. `output/clean-run.json` provides all 30 passing comparisons. This first audit used the same installed interpreter. A separate test exported the published commit `046ce79` with `git archive`, created a new Python environment, installed the pinned direct requirements from official PyPI, and ran the complete master with PDF. All 29 numerical/display/PDF-text comparisons passed, recorded in `output/fresh-environment.json`. Its complete direct and transitive dependency versions are pinned in `requirements-lock.txt`. Numerical comparisons allow relative tolerance 1e-10 and absolute tolerance 1e-12; table/macro text and plot PNGs matched exactly. Runtime metadata, PDF timestamps and the optional preexisting Stata reference are excluded from byte comparisons.

PDF pages were rendered and visually inspected as contact sheets; title/abstract and representative large tables were inspected at higher resolution. No clipped material, unresolved citations or broken tables were observed. Subsequent changes require renewed verification. Machine reproduction establishes agreement with this manuscript, not validity of every causal assumption.

# Interpretation limits affecting replication claims

Equal-budget diets remain statistically unresolved. Endline selection is not automatically ignorable; upper cash increases observed-diet retention. Sample missingness bounds do not include sampling error. Cost inputs are held fixed. Incomplete food scores differ by design from original supplied replacements, which are preserved as a sensitivity. Policy transport assumes stable costs, stable delivery and no cross-village interference. The household saving model is a possible mechanism, not structurally estimated mediation. The paper makes these restrictions explicit.
